newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Expanded Caribbean trading bloc seen by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Expanded Caribbean trading bloc seen by 2000.

text.p: The secretary-general of the Trinidad-based Association of Caribbean States said he believes the 24-nation regional group will become a full trading bloc by the end of the decade.

Simon Molina Duarte, addressing a meeting of the Caribbean Association of Industry & Commerce in Kingston Thursday evening, said the exact method by which the ACS trade regime will be established is yet to be determined, but he is confident the work will be completed shortly.

The ACS includes the 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom), a regional bloc already active on trade issues. Other ACS members are the Central American states, Mexico, Colombia, Venezuela, Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Cuba--the only trade bloc Havana has been invited to join.
The group has a total population of 200 million and a combined gross domestic product of US$500 billion.

Molina Duarte said there has "not been much advance" in the few multilateral trade negotiations the ACS has held since it was launched in August 1995, but that bilateral negotiations among ACS member states and regions are proving more fruitful.
"Bilateral agreements are another, perhaps faster way to create an ACS free trade zone," he stated.
He said Caricom is expected to begin free trade talks with the Central American Common Market, the Dominican Republic and the Andean Pact within a few weeks.

Colombia and Venezuela already have trade agreements with Caricom and Central America, and both nations are in discussions with the Dominican Republic. Santo Domingo has also been in trade talks with the Central American states.
"Before the year 2000, the ACS will be a new (trading) bloc," Molina said, based on the bilateral progress so far.

He conceded that some are questioning the need for the ACS, in light of the proposed Free Trade Area of the Americas, to be established in 2005. But he said it is more convenient for the smaller Caribbean states to approach the FTAA from as wide a regional basis as possible.

The deputy permanent secretary of the Caracas-based Latin American Economic System (SELA) Dr. Luis Alberto Rodriquez said at the conference that the ACS can serve as a "proving ground and launching pad" for Caribbean businesses in preparation for FTAA membership.
